The Peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus) is one of the most widely distributed raptors in the world, and its life history traits have been well documented across diverse populations. Eggs are typically laid in a single clutch per year, with the female producing exactly 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 eggs per clutch] and only one clutch annually [F_R_i = one clutch annually], a relatively modest reproductive output for a bird of its size. This constrained reproductive effort is thought to reflect the high energetic demands of parental care during the extended nestling period. Under the thermal conditions typical of active nesting periods (40 °C [T = 40 °C]), the fledging of young occurs at approximately 35.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 35.5 days after hatching], a developmental milestone that marks the achievement of sustained flight and the beginning of nutritional independence.

Hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] after a developmental period of about 30 days [ab = about 30 days], though reported values range from 27 to 31 days depending on local microclimatic conditions. At the moment of hatching, the wet weight at birth is approximately 37.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 37.5 grams], a modest mass typical of altricial raptor neonates. This initial size belies the rapid growth that follows, fueled by intensive biparental provisioning. The incubation length of approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days] at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] influences the timing of subsequent life-history events, as a delayed hatch can push the critical fledging and first-reproduction milestones into less favorable seasonal conditions.

Sexual maturation in the Peregrine falcon follows a predictable developmental trajectory under the thermal regime characteristic of its active season (40 °C [T = 40 °C]). Puberty is reached at 106.5 days after hatching [tp = 106.5 days after hatching], although some field records indicate a narrower window of 32 to 35 days for initial gonadal activation at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This attainment of reproductive maturity is notably later than in many smaller falcon species, reflecting the extended period required for full somatic growth before reproductive competence is achieved. During this period, the growing juvenile undergoes significant changes in body composition and flight muscle development, gradually transitioning from a fully dependent nestling to a capable predator.

Substantial sexual dimorphism in body mass is a hallmark of this species. Adult females attain an asymptotic body mass of 865.6 g [Wwi = 865.6 g], while males, exhibiting marked sexual dimorphism, plateau at 579.2 g [Wwi = 579.2 g]. The nearly 300-gram difference between the sexes is among the most pronounced within the genus Falco and is thought to facilitate niche partitioning, allowing the larger female to take a broader range of prey, including larger avian species. These maximum recorded body masses in adults are typically achieved during the second year of life, following the completion of the juvenile growth phase and the onset of full physiological maturity.

Longevity and the timing of first reproduction are critical parameters for understanding population dynamics in this long-lived raptor. The initial wet weight of newly hatched chicks is about 47 g [Ww0 = about 47 g], a value that reflects the residual yolk reserves available to the neonate during its first few days of life. At a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for wild individuals is 9125 days [am = 9125 days]. First successful breeding events typically occur at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This age at first reproduction is relatively early for a species of this body size and is facilitated by the falcon's rapid juvenile development and early attainment of hunting proficiency.
